explain.summary: When Tomás gulps a cold smoothie, the cold hits the roof of his mouth fast. Small blood vessels there tighten and then rush open, and a big face nerve passes the signal on — his brain feels it as an ache in his forehead, even though nothing touched it. His brain doesn't actually get colder. The ache fades within seconds, faster if he warms the roof of his mouth with his tongue.
rules: Faster gulps and colder drinks cool the roof of the mouth more.
Below a small amount of cooling there's no ache — that's why slow sips are fine.
The ache halves about every 12 seconds; a warm tongue makes it fade about twice as fast.
His brain stays at body temperature the whole time.

source.fact: Cold on the roof of the mouth makes small blood vessels tighten then rapidly open; nerve signals through the trigeminal nerve are felt as pain in the head.
Brain freeze lasts from a few seconds to a few minutes; pressing the tongue on the roof of the mouth can stop it; eating cold foods slowly may avoid it.
It usually lasts under two minutes and is not harmful.

choice.what: Roof-of-mouth cooling = gulp speed × (98.6 − drink temperature) × 0.35
choice.why: A simple way to show faster gulps and colder drinks both cool the palate more; the 0.35 is a teaching value.

choice.what: No ache until the palate cools by more than 4°F
choice.why: Shows clue 2: slow sips never hurt.

choice.what: The ache halves every 12 seconds, every 5 seconds with a warm tongue
choice.why: Matches clue 4 (gone in about half a minute) and clue 3 (the tongue makes it fade faster).

choice.what: Drink temperature and sensitivity are adjustable
choice.why: Lets you see why his friend gets the same thing from ice cream, and why some people rarely get it.

illustrative: Tomás's gulp speed, his 25°F smoothie and the 0–10 ache scale are made up for a fictional story.
provenance.studying: Scientists still debate exactly what causes brain freeze. The leading idea is blood vessels in the roof of the mouth tightening and then rushing open, but it is hard to study because each one is over so quickly.

citations.title: What happens during a brain freeze, and is it harmful?
citations.supports: The cause is debated; the leading idea is that cold on the roof of the mouth makes small blood vessels tighten then rapidly open, and nerve signals via the trigeminal nerve are felt as pain in the head (referred pain); it usually lasts under two minutes; eat very cold foods slowly.

citations.title: Brain freeze
citations.supports: Brain freeze is a cold-induced headache lasting a few seconds to a few minutes; blood vessels in the roof of the mouth narrow; pressing your tongue on the roof of your mouth can stop it; eating and drinking cold foods slowly may avoid it.

citations.title: Body temperature norms
citations.supports: Average normal body temperature is generally accepted as 98.6°F (37°C); normal can range from about 97°F to 99°F.

does: Shows the ache growing with how much cold hits the roof of the mouth, and how fast
Shows the ache fading within half a minute
Shows slow sips causing little or no ache
doesnt: Measure any real person — the numbers are illustrative teaching values
Show the exact timing of the blood vessels; scientists are still studying how it works
Say anything about other kinds of headaches
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Headaches that come without anything cold, or don't go away, are a reason to tell an adult.
